issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette: Sai, a 26-year-old South Eastern Asian man with a history of divorce and currently working as a bank teller in downtown Los Angeles, sought help after experiencing escalating symptoms following an encounter with terrorism. The traumatic event that has significantly impacted Sai's life occurred about six months ago when he was at work during a robbery attempt by individuals who were later identified as part of a terrorist cell. On the day of the incident, Sai had just started his shift in the bank, which is located in a bustling commercial area. Suddenly, masked figures burst into the bank, brandishing weapons and shouting demands. The chaos and fear were overwhelming; customers screamed, and staff members cowered behind their desks. Despite the danger, Sai felt an urge to help others, leading him to assist several clients by ushering them towards safer areas of the bank. However, during the ordeal, he also found himself momentarily frozen in place, unable to move or think clearly. In the days following the event, Sai began to experience a range of symptoms that seemed to intensify over time. He started working excessively long hours at the bank, often staying late into the evening and even showing up on his days off. His rationale was clear: he needed to keep himself busy to avoid being alone with his thoughts. Being alone, as he had come to believe, only amplified the haunting memories of that day. Additionally, Sai avoided any form of emotional closeness or intimacy. The idea of allowing someone else into his life felt too risky; he feared that forming a bond would inevitably lead to more pain and vulnerability. Sai also found himself trying hard not to think about the trauma, even though it seemed to haunt him relentlessly. At night, he woke up multiple times to check whether he was safe, often finding himself looking out the window or behind his door with his heart racing. The fear of someone following him led Sai to frequently glance over his shoulder on his way home from work, a habit that had become so ingrained it felt almost automatic. The negative appraisals Sai held were profoundly distressing. He believed he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. His role as a bank teller, once a source of pride and stability, now seemed insignificant compared to his perceived failures during the robbery. Moreover, he viewed his actions-both helping others and being momentarily frozen in fear-as betrayals of who he thought himself to be. The inconsistency between his values and his behaviors during the event left him feeling deeply flawed. The strain of these thoughts and behaviors began to take a toll on Sai's personal life as well. He had recently started dating again but found it incredibly difficult to maintain any sort of emotional connection with his partner, whom he referred to only as "her." The relationship suffered because he was unable to open up or trust her fully. What finally brought Sai to seek help was a combination of increasing irritability and the realization that his work-life balance had become dangerously imbalanced. At home, small frustrations could escalate into angry outbursts, and at work, he found himself snapping at colleagues over minor issues. The tension between maintaining control and breaking down under stress became too much to bear. Sai was most afraid of becoming a shell of the person he once was-a man defined by his fear rather than his actions or values. Yet, despite this fear, there was hope. He sought therapy with the belief that understanding and processing his trauma could help him regain some sense of control over his life. Sai hoped to find ways to manage his symptoms without sacrificing who he truly was. The journey ahead would be challenging, but Sai's desire for change was palpable. Through therapy, he aimed to reconstruct a narrative of himself where the events of that day did not overshadow his strengths and capabilities. By addressing the complex interplay of trauma responses, negative appraisals, and avoidance behaviors, Sai hoped to reclaim a sense of self-worth and control over his life.
